the observed (uncor-rected for extinction) luminosity function of SNe in a volume-limited survey is significantly non-Gaussian, and there are large differences between the luminosity functions of different SN subclasses.

the observed (unextinguished) LFs of SNe Ia and II-P are well described by Gaussian distributions, but that the other subclasses have more complicated distributions that are not well described by Gaussian functions, and that the observed fractions of SNe IIn, IIb, and II-L in a complete SN II sample are 9, 12, and 10 per cent, respectively.

the observed LFs of SNe are not well represented with a Gaussian, the LFs of SNE Ia, Ibc, II, and IIn are significantly different, the LFs are more “standard” and have less scatter when the observation interval decreases, and there are notable differences in LFs of SNa in different host-galaxy sizes, inclinations, and Hubble types.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed SN LF is very complicated and depends on the SN type, the galaxy type, the observation time interval, and the galaxy inclination.
the LFs of SNe are complex, and that the luminosity distribution and host-galaxy extinction are important issues to consider in the calculation of SN rates.
SNe Ia and Ibc have very similar LFs, and the LFs of SNe II and IIn are different from each other, but the LFs of the different SN subclasses in the same galaxy type are very similar.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LFs of different SNe are not standard and are not well represented with a simple Gaussian distribution.
the SN LFs, the SN rates and the observed fractions for different subclasses in a magnitudesurvey are significantly affected by the observation interval, the host-galaxy luminosity and extinction.

the LFs of nearby SNe are not well represented as Gaussian distributions.
the observed SN LF is not well represented by the Gaussian distribution, and the LFs for different SN subclasses are not the same.
